att-01.answer: The Transformer achieved a BLEU score of 28.4 on the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task [1][3].

att-02.answer: The Transformer achieved a BLEU score of 41.0 on the WMT 2014 English-to-French translation task [1][2]. The document states that the model was trained for 3.5 days on eight GPUs [3].

att-03.answer: The Transformer encoder stack is composed of N = 6 identical layers. [1]

att-04.answer: The Transformer employs h = 8 parallel attention heads, with each head using dimensions dk = dv = dmodel/h = 64 [2].

att-05.answer: The Transformer learning rate schedule used 4,000 warmup steps [1].

att-06.answer: The Transformer models were trained on one machine equipped with 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs [10].

att-07.answer: The base Transformer models were trained for a total of 100,000 steps, which took 12 hours [1][2].

att-08.answer: The Transformer authors used a label smoothing value of 0.1 [1]. This technique hurt perplexity by making the model more unsure, but it improved both accuracy and the BLEU score [1].

att-09.answer: The Transformer uses sine and cosine functions of different frequencies for its positional encodings [1]. Specifically, the positional encoding is defined by the formulas PE(pos, 2i) = sin(pos/10000^(2i/dmodel)) and PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos(pos/10000^(2i/dmodel)) [1]. The authors chose this sinusoidal version because it may allow the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than those encountered during training [4].

att-10.answer: The per-layer computational complexity of a self-attention layer is O(n² · d), whereas a recurrent layer has a complexity of O(n · d²) [3]. Self-attention layers are faster than recurrent layers when the sequence length n is less than the representation dimension d [1].

bert-01.answer: BERTBASE contains 110M parameters and BERTLARGE contains 340M parameters [1][3].

bert-02.answer: BERT masks 15% of all WordPiece tokens in each sequence at random during pre-training [1][3].

bert-03.answer: When BERT selects a token for masked prediction, it replaces the token with the [MASK] token 80% of the time, a random token 10% of the time, or leaves the token unchanged 10% of the time [1]. This specific distribution is also detailed in the ablation studies as 80% MASK, 10% SAME, and 10% RND [8].

bert-04.answer: BERTLARGE obtained a score of 80.5 on the official GLUE leaderboard [1][3]. Additionally, BERTBASE and BERTLARGE achieved average accuracy improvements of 4.5% and 7.0% respectively over the prior state of the art [3].

bert-05.answer: BERT reached a Test F1 of 93.2 on SQuAD v1.1 [1][4].

bert-06.answer: BERT reached a Test F1 of 83.1 on SQuAD v2.0 [1][2].

bert-07.answer: BERT was pre-trained on the BooksCorpus, which contains 800 million words, and English Wikipedia, which contains 2,500 million words [1][4].

bert-08.answer: In BERT's next sentence prediction task, 50% of the time sentence B is the actual next sentence that follows sentence A, and 50% of the time it is a random sentence from the corpus [1][7].

bert-09.answer: BERT uses a WordPiece vocabulary of 30,000 tokens [1].

bert-10.answer: BERT was pre-trained for 1,000,000 steps with a batch size of 128,000 words [2].

sbert-01.answer: With BERT, finding the most similar pair among 10,000 sentences takes about 65 hours, whereas with SBERT it takes about 5 seconds [1][3][5].

sbert-02.answer: Sentence-BERT uses siamese and triplet network structures to derive semantically meaningful sentence embeddings [1][2]. These structures are applied to fine-tune the pretrained BERT or RoBERTa networks [2][9].

sbert-03.answer: Sentence-BERT experiments with three pooling strategies: using the output of the CLS-token, computing the mean of all output vectors (MEAN strategy), and computing a max-over-time of the output vectors (MAX strategy) [1].

sbert-04.answer: The default pooling strategy in SBERT is MEAN. [1][2][3]

sbert-05.answer: The SNLI dataset contains 570,000 sentence pairs, while the MultiNLI dataset contains 430,000 sentence pairs [1].

sbert-06.answer: To fine-tune SBERT on NLI data, a batch size of 16, the Adam optimizer, and a learning rate of 2e−5 were used [1].

sbert-07.answer: In SBERT's triplet objective, the Euclidean distance is used as the metric, and the margin ϵ is set to 1. [1]

sbert-08.answer: The smart batching strategy in SBERT groups sentences with similar lengths together and pads them only to the longest element within a mini-batch [1]. This approach drastically reduces the computational overhead associated with padding tokens [1].

sbert-09.answer: SBERT can be fine-tuned in less than 20 minutes [1].

sbert-10.answer: The Sentence-BERT paper evaluates argument similarity on the Argument Facet Similarity (AFS) corpus [2][3]. This corpus contains 6,000 annotated sentential argument pairs from social media dialogs on topics such as gun control, gay marriage, and the death penalty [2].

dpr-01.answer: The Dense Passage Retriever outperforms BM25 by 9% to 19% absolute in terms of top-20 passage retrieval accuracy [1]. For example, on the Natural Questions dataset, the top-20 accuracy is 78.4% for DPR compared to 59.1% for BM25 [6][8].

dpr-02.answer: The documents do not specify the exact length of the passages, only noting that they are split into "equal lengths" and that fixed-length passages perform better than natural paragraphs [2][10]. The total number of passages, denoted as M, can be very large, with the specific experiments described in the paper using 21 million passages [1].

dpr-03.answer: The documents indicate that the RAG paper used the December 2018 Wikipedia dump, splitting articles into disjoint 100-word chunks to create a total of 21 million documents [1]. Similarly, the Dense Passage Retrieval (DPR) paper utilized the English Wikipedia dump from December 20, 2018, as its source for answering questions [2]. While the Self-RAG paper primarily used 2018 English Wikipedia embeddings, it switched to a December 2020 preprocessed corpus for the PopQA dataset to address missing recent entities [4].

dpr-04.answer: DPR measures similarity by applying a dot product to the d-dimensional vectors of the question and the passage, defined as sim(q, p) = EQ(q)⊺EP(p) [1]. This decomposable similarity function allows the passage representations to be precomputed, and the system retrieves the k passages with vectors closest to the question vector [1]. While other decomposable functions like cosine and Euclidean L2 distance exist, the paper notes that L2 performs comparably to dot product, and both are superior to cosine [2].

dpr-05.answer: The retrieval component in RAG is based on DPR, which follows a bi-encoder architecture [2]. At run-time, DPR uses a different encoder to map the input question to a vector and retrieves passages whose vectors are closest to the question vector [1]. The similarity between the question and passage is defined using the dot product of their vectors [1].

dpr-06.answer: The main DPR model was trained with a batch size of 128, using in-batch negative settings that included one additional BM25 negative passage per question [1].

dpr-07.answer: DPR trained using only 1,000 examples already outperforms BM25 [2][3].

dpr-08.answer: DPR can process 995.0 questions per second at run time [1].

dpr-09.answer: Computing dense embeddings for 21 million passages takes roughly 8.8 hours on 8 GPUs [1].

dpr-10.answer: BM25 performs better than DPR on SQuAD because the questions were written by annotators after seeing the passages, resulting in high lexical overlap that favors BM25's keyword matching [2]. Additionally, the SQuAD data was collected from a limited set of over 500 Wikipedia articles, creating an extremely narrow distribution of training examples that introduces unwanted bias [1][2].

colbert-01.answer: ColBERT is more than 170× faster and requires 14,000× fewer FLOPs per query than existing BERT-based models [1][2].

colbert-02.answer: When used for re-ranking, ColBERT delivers over 170× speedup relative to existing BERT-based models [1]. This speedup is accompanied by a requirement for 14,000× fewer FLOPs [1].

colbert-03.answer: The number of embeddings per query is fixed at Nq = 32 in ColBERT [1].

colbert-04.answer: ColBERT typically uses an embedding dimension of 128 [1][3].

colbert-05.answer: ColBERT prepends the special token [Q] to queries and the special token [D] to documents [3][4].

colbert-06.answer: I do not know. The provided excerpts do not state that the ColBERT document encoder "filters out" any specific content. They only state that the document encoder segments a document into its constituent tokens and prepends BERT's start token [CLS] and a special token [D] [8].

colbert-07.answer: Query augmentation in ColBERT is a step where the padded sequence of input tokens is passed into BERT to produce query-based embeddings at the positions corresponding to masked tokens [1]. This mechanism serves as a soft, differentiable way to learn to expand queries with new terms or re-weigh existing terms based on their importance for matching the query [1]. The ablation results indicate that this operation is essential for ColBERT's effectiveness, as the model without query augmentation achieves a noticeably lower MRR@10 [2][3].

colbert-08.answer:
The provided excerpts do not explicitly state the specific faiss index type (e.g., IVF, HNSW) used by ColBERT for end-to-end retrieval. They only mention that ColBERT uses a faiss index, sets the number of partitions to P = 2,000, and searches the nearest p = 10 to each query embedding [2][8].

colbert-09.answer: ColBERT can index the MS MARCO collection in about three hours [1][2].

colbert-10.answer: ColBERT is evaluated on the MS MARCO and TREC CAR (TREC Complex Answer Retrieval) passage search collections [1][7].

rag-01.answer: The primary difference is that RAG-Sequence uses the same retrieved document to generate the entire output sequence, whereas RAG-Token can draw a different latent document for each individual target token [3][6]. This allows RAG-Token to combine content from several documents when producing an answer, while RAG-Sequence treats the retrieved document as a single latent variable for the whole sequence [2][6].

rag-02.answer: RAG uses BART-large as its generator, which has 406M parameters [1].

rag-03.answer: Each Wikipedia article is split into disjoint 100-word chunks, resulting in a total of 21 million documents [1].

rag-04.answer: The RAG system uses a dense vector index built from a single Wikipedia dump, specifically the December 2018 dump, which is split into disjoint 100-word chunks to create 21 million documents [1]. The retrieval component is based on DPR (Dense Passage Retrieval), which employs a bi-encoder architecture to compute embeddings for documents and queries [8]. During training, the system retrieves the top k documents for each query, with k set to either 5 or 10, while the test time k is selected using development data [1].

rag-05.answer: In the original RAG model, the parametric memory (a pre-trained seq2seq transformer like BART) and the non-parametric memory (a dense vector index accessed by a pre-trained neural retriever like DPR) are combined in a probabilistic model that is trained end-to-end [2]. This implies that both the retriever and the generator components are fine-tuned during training rather than kept fixed [2]. In contrast, SELF-RAG trains an arbitrary LM to learn to use retrieval on-demand, but the excerpts do not explicitly state whether the retriever itself is fine-tuned or kept fixed in that specific system [4].

rag-06.answer: In the human evaluation of Jeopardy question generation, RAG was found to be more factual than BART in 42.7% of cases [1][3].

rag-07.answer: The RAG authors demonstrated index hot-swapping by building an index using the DrQA Wikipedia dump from December 2016 and comparing its outputs to those from a newer index from December 2018 [1]. They specifically prepared a list of 82 world leaders who had changed to illustrate how knowledge can be easily updated at test time without retraining [1].

rag-08.answer: The compressed RAG document index requires 36GB of CPU memory [1].

rag-09.answer: Thorough Decoding is a procedure for RAG-Sequence where, to estimate the probability of a hypothesis $y$, an additional forward pass is run for each retrieved document $z$ for which $y$ does not appear in the beam search results [1][6]. The generator probability is then multiplied by the retriever probability $p_\eta(z|x)$, and these probabilities are summed across the beams to compute the marginals [1][6]. This approach is used because the RAG-Sequence likelihood does not break into a conventional per-token likelihood, preventing the use of a single standard beam search [6].

rag-10.answer: On the FEVER fact verification task, RAG achieves results within 4.3% of state-of-the-art models [1][2][3].

beir-01.answer: The BEIR benchmark includes 18 datasets and evaluates 10 retrieval systems [5].

beir-02.answer: BEIR covers nine different retrieval tasks [1][2].

beir-03.answer: BEIR reports Normalised Cumulative Discount Gain (nDCG@k) as the evaluation metric for all datasets. [1]

beir-04.answer: The BEIR benchmark concludes that BM25 is a robust and strong baseline for zero-shot text retrieval, often outperforming many neural approaches in generalization despite underperforming them on in-domain tasks like MS MARCO [1][3][7]. While re-ranking and late-interaction models achieve the best average zero-shot performance, they do so at high computational costs, whereas BM25 remains computationally efficient [1][7]. Additionally, the benchmark notes that in-domain performance is not a good indicator for out-of-domain generalization, a fact highlighted by BM25's strong generalization capabilities [3][7].

beir-05.answer: Re-ranking and late-interaction based models achieve the best zero-shot performance on the BEIR benchmark, but they do so at high computational costs and high latency (over 350 ms) [1][2]. In contrast, dense and sparse-retrieval models are computationally more efficient but often underperform these approaches [1][2].

beir-06.answer: In the BEIR study, the ColBERT index for BioASQ requires approximately 900GB, whereas the BM25 index requires only 18GB [1][2].

beir-07.answer: No, according to BEIR, in-domain performance does not predict how well a retrieval model generalizes in a zero-shot setup [1]. The study found that in-domain performance does not correlate well with generalization capabilities, and many approaches that outperform BM25 in-domain perform poorly on the BEIR datasets [1][3].

beir-08.answer: TAS-B is a bi-encoder model trained with Balanced Topic Aware Sampling using dual supervision from a cross-encoder and a ColBERT model [9]. It utilizes a training setup that combines in-domain batch negatives with Margin-MSE losses and strong ensemble teachers in a Knowledge Distillation setup [6]. This approach allows TAS-B to provide the best zero-shot generalization performance among its dense counterparts, outperforming ANCE on 14 out of 18 datasets and DPR on 17 out of 18 datasets [6].

beir-09.answer: DocT5query is a document expansion technique that uses a T5 model trained on MS MARCO to generate synthetic queries, which are then appended to the original document to improve lexical search performance [2][4]. It identifies document expansion terms using a sequence-to-sequence model that generates possible queries for which the given document would be relevant [4].

beir-10.answer: The BEIR authors notice a strong lexical bias in the benchmark datasets, which likely arises because lexical models are predominantly used during the annotation or creation of the datasets [2]. This bias is also described as a selection bias, where candidates for annotation are retrieved using lexical-based systems, causing unseen documents to be automatically assumed irrelevant [1][7].

hyde-01.answer: HyDE stands for Hypothetical Document Embeddings [2]. Its first step is to feed the query to a generative model and instruct it to "write a document that answers the question," creating a hypothetical document [9].

hyde-02.answer: HyDE is implemented using InstructGPT, which is a GPT-3 model from the instruct series (specifically text-davinci-003) [3]. The paper also notes that HyDE can be used with other instruction-following language models, such as the 52-billion Cohere model and the 11-billion FLAN-T5-xxl model [1].

hyde-03.answer: In HyDE, an unsupervised contrastively learned encoder, such as Contriever, turns the hypothetical document into an embedding vector [1][2]. This encoder acts as a lossy compressor or dense bottleneck that filters out incorrect or hallucinated details from the generated document [2][5].

hyde-04.answer: HyDE uses a sampling temperature of 0.7 when generating documents with InstructGPT [1][6].

hyde-05.answer: HyDE is evaluated on Swahili, Korean, Japanese, and Bengali [3][4][8].

hyde-06.answer: The web search query sets used to evaluate HyDE are TREC DL19 and TREC DL20 [8]. These datasets are based on the MS-MARCO dataset [8].

hyde-07.answer: HyDE deals with false details by using an unsupervised contrastively learned encoder to convert the hypothetical document into a dense embedding vector [1]. This encoder acts as a lossy compressor or dense bottleneck that filters out the incorrect or hallucinated details [3][4]. The resulting vector is then used to retrieve similar real documents from the corpus, effectively grounding the generated content to actual data [1][3].
